name: Victor Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential and won't be traced back to you. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I run the accounts payable team at Northgate Foods, the big food wholesaler, so nine people who check supplier invoices against orders and get suppliers paid on time. My day starts at eight with a stand-up, then it's mostly exceptions: an invoice for 400 cases of tinned tomatoes when we got 380, a supplier shouting about a late payment. Afternoons are reports for the finance director and one-to-ones with my team.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing a mess and seeing the overdue payments report go green on a Friday, which just means nobody's been waiting too long for their money. What wears me out is month end, when everything lands at once and I'm in till seven two nights running. I'm 27, I live with my partner Anika, she's a hospital pharmacist, and we're saving for a flat, so the pay is worth the long nights for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly what I see at Northgate today. The invoice-scanning tool reads the paper invoices for us, and it still gets the supplier name wrong about one time in ten. If all the hype only buys us a slightly better invoice scanner, my job at the food wholesaler looks much like it does today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, the tools help with the boring bits and we keep making the judgement calls. With friends I'd probably joke that all the hype bought us a slightly better scanner. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not fully. Northgate has been squeezing head office costs for two years anyway, and they didn't replace two people who left my team last spring. So even with no big AI change, the pressure on headcount carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and go for the senior manager role that should open when my boss Grant retires in about two years. I'd keep putting 1,200 a month into the flat deposit fund. And I'd start the part-qualified accountant course Northgate pays for, because that helps me move up whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled, to be honest. We've got almost a year of spending saved, and there are plenty of finance jobs in the city if Northgate ever gets silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned two people weren't replaced. What happened to their work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It got spread across the other seven, plus the scanning tool picked up some of the typing. Priya, who's been there longest, took on the dairy suppliers and she's tired. I keep telling the finance director we're one sick week away from late payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave Northgate, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Grant's job went to someone outside and I was stuck at the same level for three more years. I'm not restless, but I'm also not going to sit still at 30. A competitor offered me a chat last year, and I kept the number.

say: AI helps with the **boring bits**, and my team keeps making the judgement calls.
All the hype bought us a **slightly better scanner**, I'd joke with friends.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but head office was already being squeezed for cost.
Two people who left my team **weren't replaced**, so headcount pressure carries on anyway.
do: Go for **Grant's senior manager role** when my boss retires in about two years.
Keep saving **1,200 a month** towards the flat deposit with Anika.
Start the **part-qualified accountant course** that Northgate pays for.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with almost a year of spending saved and plenty of finance jobs nearby.
S0.quote: If all the hype only buys us a slightly better invoice scanner, my job at the food wholesaler looks much like it does today.
fieldNote: His **real worry** is cost-cutting, not AI; two unreplaced leavers already stretch the team.
His ambition is **steady, not restless**: he kept a competitor's number but isn't calling it.
**Savings** and a **busy job market** keep him calm despite month-end strain.

steps.text: Apply for the senior manager role when Grant retires
Keep putting 1,200 a month into the flat deposit fund
Start the part-qualified accountant course Northgate pays for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's much closer to home. Checking is literally what my team does all day, so if software gets good at checking, nine people becomes four pretty quickly. Does the invoice match the order, does the price match the contract, that's the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say what the finance director wants to hear, that we'll embrace it and move people into new roles. To friends I'd be more honest and say accounts payable is going to be one of the first desks to shrink. I might share an article or two on my work profile, but nothing with my own opinion in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my team gets cut by half within two or three years, and a team of four doesn't need its own manager. They'd fold us into the team that chases customer payments and keep one manager for both. I'd have maybe a 50-50 chance of being that one, and the other manager, Sunita, has been there longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd ask to lead the rollout of whatever new invoice software they buy, so my name is on it. I'd finish the accountant course faster, maybe by doubling up modules next year. And I'd quietly update my CV and call that competitor back, just to know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach, honestly. Not panic, because we've got savings and there are jobs around, but I'd hate to be the manager who runs the cuts and then gets cut himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya. She's 52, she's brilliant with suppliers, and she's never used anything beyond the scanning tool and a spreadsheet. If the checking goes to software, I don't know where she lands. I'd try hard to move her into supplier relations, where the people part still matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for the flat with Anika?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably hold off buying for a year. Locking into a mortgage the same month my team is being restructured feels like asking for trouble. Anika's job at the hospital is safe, so we wouldn't panic, but I'd want to see where I land first.

say: We'll **embrace it** and move people, which is what the finance director wants to hear.
Accounts payable will be one of the **first desks** to shrink, I'd tell friends.
think: My team probably **gets cut by half** within two or three years.
A merged finance team keeps **one manager**, and Sunita has been there longer than me.
do: Ask to **lead the rollout** of the new invoice software so my name is on it.
Finish the **accountant course** faster by doubling up modules next year.
Update my CV and **call the competitor back** to know where I stand.
feel: **Uneasy in my stomach**, though savings and nearby jobs keep it short of panic.
I'd hate to **run the cuts** and then get cut myself.
S1.quote: Checking is literally what my team does all day, so if software gets good at checking, nine people becomes four pretty quickly.
fieldNote: He sees his team's core work, **checking invoices**, named directly as what AI takes first.
His **public line** follows the company script; privately he expects a merged team and one manager.
**Priya**, a 52-year-old team member, is the person he worries about most.
Anika's **secure hospital job** softens the blow but delays the flat purchase.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the rollout of the new invoice software
Double up accountant course modules to finish a year early
Call back the competitor who offered a chat last year
Hold off buying the flat with Anika for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even finish the accountant course. If AI can do almost any thinking work, then invoices, reports, supplier emails, all of it goes, and so does managing the people who did it. There's nothing hands-on in my head-office job to buy me those extra three years before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd probably say we need to slow down and think about this, and that governments have to get involved. At work I'd keep my head down and say whatever kept the team calm. Online I'd stay quiet, because I wouldn't want a future employer reading me panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd expect to be out of a job within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. Northgate is a low-margin business and they'd jump at cutting head office. A finance degree and four years of managing an invoice team would be worth very little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd stop spending on anything big: no new car, no holiday to Lisbon we've been planning. I'd move the deposit savings into easy-access cash so it's there if I'm out of work. Then I'd look at what's still people-facing for a few years, maybe operations in the warehouses, where the robots don't arrive till 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I'd be lying awake doing the maths on how long the savings last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouses. Would you really go from head office to the warehouse floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go as a shift manager, not packing boxes, but yes. I've done two days there for a stock count and I liked it more than I expected. It's a step down in pay, maybe 20 percent, but it's three more years of a wage while I work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Anika talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly. Whether we can live on her salary alone, which we could, just about, if we gave up the flat idea. She'd tell me not to panic, and I'd tell her I'm not panicking, and we'd both know I was.

say: Governments need to **slow this down** and think it through.
At work I'd **keep my head down** and keep the team calm.
Online I'd **stay quiet**, so no future employer sees me panicking.
think: I'd expect to be **out of a job** within a year of AGI arriving.
Northgate is **low-margin** and would jump at cutting head office.
My finance degree and **invoice team experience** would be worth very little.
do: Cancel **big spending**, including a new car and the Lisbon holiday.
Move the **deposit savings into cash** in case I'm out of work.
Look for **warehouse shift manager** jobs, where robots arrive around 2031.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake working out how long the savings last.
S2.quote: There's nothing hands-on in my head-office job to buy me those extra three years before the robots arrive.
fieldNote: He sees **no hands-on buffer** in his own job, so the 2028 date hits him directly.
The **warehouse floor** is his bridge: a 20 percent pay cut for three more years of wages.
Anika's salary is the **household backstop**, and he admits they'd both see through his calm.

steps.text: Cancel the Lisbon holiday and the new car
Move the flat deposit savings into easy-access cash
Apply for warehouse shift manager jobs before the robots arrive
Plan to live on Anika's hospital salary if laid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes things a lot for me. I'd be 32 when it lands, I'd have the accountant qualification, and I'd have had time to move. It's still the same ending for an invoice team, but I wouldn't be caught standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a wake-up call and companies should use the five years to retrain people properly. At work I'd push for Northgate to plan it openly instead of springing it on us. With friends I'd probably say finance people need to get out of pure desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my current job is gone by 2031 either way. The question is whether I'm still in it when it goes. Five years is enough to land somewhere less exposed, if I start in the first year and don't kid myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the qualification and then ask for a move into operations finance, the people who sit with the warehouse managers and plan stock. I'd keep saving hard, maybe 1,500 a month, and we'd still buy a smaller flat, because a home is something AI can't take off you. I'd learn the new AI tools properly instead of dabbling, so I'm the one setting them up, not the one being replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but more in control. Like seeing a storm on the forecast a week out instead of when it's on top of you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller flat instead of waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because renting with no job is worse than owning with a small mortgage. If we buy a two-bed in the cheaper part of town, Anika's salary alone covers the mortgage. That was her idea, and she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when it arrives, what's left for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'm not sure. Maybe running a site, where you're managing people and lorries and real problems, until the robots come around 2034. Past that I can't see clearly, and I'd rather admit that than make something up.

say: This is a **wake-up call**, and firms should use five years to retrain people.
Northgate should **plan it openly** instead of springing it on staff.
think: My current job is **gone by 2031** either way.
Five years is enough to **land somewhere less exposed** if I start early.
do: Finish the **qualification**, then move into **operations finance**.
Save about **1,500 a month** and still buy a smaller flat.
Learn the AI tools **properly** so I'm setting them up, not replaced by them.
feel: **Nervous** but more **in control**, like seeing a storm on the forecast a week out.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to land somewhere less exposed, if I start in the first year and don't kid myself.
fieldNote: The **five-year window** turns his fear into a plan he can start in year one.
He treats a **small mortgage** as safer than renting with no job, which was Anika's idea.
Beyond 2034 he **honestly can't see** a path, and says so plainly.

steps.text: Finish the accountant qualification in the first year
Ask to move into operations finance with the warehouse managers
Learn the new AI invoice tools well enough to set them up
Buy a smaller two-bed flat that Anika's salary alone covers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd be 37, probably with kids by then, and I'd have a whole career move behind me before it arrives. It still ends the same way for desk work, but a decade is long enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's use it, and I'd mean it. At work I'd tell my team to start learning now rather than waiting. I'd probably be the annoying friend who keeps bringing it up at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years of warning is scary in a different way, because it's easy to waste. I know myself, I'd tell myself there's plenty of time and then suddenly it's 2033. The kids part worries me too, because they'd be small exactly when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a deadline: out of pure finance desk work by 2030. I'd use the first year to get the qualification and then try a role closer to the business, maybe running a distribution site. And I'd start putting money into an index fund every month, because if the companies get richer from AI, I'd like a slice of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Relieved there's time, but uneasy that I'll waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change when you and Anika have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might push it a little later, maybe 2030 instead of 2028, once I've made the move. Anika would say that's an excuse, and she'd have a point. I wouldn't want my first year as a dad to also be my last year with a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya, the colleague you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To use the time to get into supplier relations or something where people trust a face. She's got 15 working years left, so ten years of warning really matters for her. I'd help her write the internal application myself.

say: We've got time, so **let's use it**, and I'd mean that.
I'd tell my team to **start learning now** instead of waiting.
think: Ten years of warning is **easy to waste**, and I know I'd drift.
Our **future kids** would be small exactly when AGI hits.
do: Set a **2030 deadline** to leave pure finance desk work.
Get the qualification, then try **running a distribution site**.
Put money into an **index fund** every month to share in AI gains.
feel: **Relieved** there's time, but **uneasy** I'll waste it.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is scary in a different way, because it's easy to waste.
fieldNote: For him the long window's main danger is **complacency**, not shock.
He'd **delay children** to around 2030 and admits Anika might call it an excuse.
He thinks of **Priya's 15 working years** and would help her move internally.

steps.text: Get the accountant qualification during the first year
Apply to run a Northgate distribution site by 2030
Put money into an index fund every month
Push having children back to around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to finish a qualification, never mind change careers, and a head-office job like mine has no hands-on part to hide in. What would help is employers being honest early, plus proper paid retraining, not a two-hour online module. And some kind of wage top-up for people who move into lower-paid jobs while they retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like being the manager in the middle. Nobody trains you to tell nine people their jobs are changing while you're scared for your own. I think a lot of managers my age will have to do it.

headlineQuote: Nobody trains you to tell nine people their jobs are changing while you're scared for your own.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old accounts payable manager** at Northgate Foods, running nine invoice checkers.
He lives with Anika, a **hospital pharmacist**, and they're saving for a flat.
He's **calm in AI Plateau**, where cost-cutting rather than AI is his main pressure.
Steady Disruption and **AGI by 2028** hit hard, because invoice checking is pure thinking work.
Longer warnings give him **a plan**, though he fears wasting a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to finish a qualification or change careers.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest warning** from employers and proper **paid retraining**.
A **wage top-up** for people who take lower-paid jobs while they retrain.
